# secret-server

> Self-hosted secrets manager: a single Go binary with SQLite storage. Secrets
> are AES-256-GCM encrypted at rest and vended read-only through one public
> endpoint to GitHub Actions workflows (OIDC) and machine-token clients.
> Everything else (management API + web UI) is human-only behind Cloudflare
> Access.

## Fetching secrets (the only public API)

    GET {{BASE_URL}}/github/v1/secrets
    Authorization: Bearer <credential>

The bearer credential is one of:

- A GitHub Actions OIDC JWT (requested by the workflow via its identity token
  endpoint).
- A machine token (prefix `sst_`) issued by an admin, for clients that cannot
  present an OIDC JWT. The `sst_` prefix alone selects the validation path;
  both credential types share this one route.

The response is a flat JSON object mapping secret name to plaintext value.
Secret names are globally unique server-wide, so there is no nesting and no
collision handling:

    {"DB_URL": "postgres://...", "API_KEY": "..."}

A valid credential that is authorized for no secrets gets `{}` (HTTP 200).
A missing or invalid credential gets HTTP 401 with `{"error": "..."}`.

Machine-token example:

    curl -fsSL -H "Authorization: Bearer $SECRET_SERVER_TOKEN" \
      {{BASE_URL}}/github/v1/secrets

The Agent Host control plane also uses HEAD/POST
`{{BASE_URL}}/github/v1/push-provenance` with a machine token whose separate
push-attestation capability is enabled. That route is not for workflows or
agent containers.

## How access is authorized

- Secrets live in a tree of nodes: `secret` leaves and `group` composites.
- Access policies are pattern-match rules attached to nodes. Each policy holds
  SQLite GLOB patterns of three kinds: `repository`, `ref`, and `actor`.
- An OIDC request matches a policy only if at least one pattern of EACH kind
  matches the repository, ref, and resolved actor. Actor patterns may target a
  login or an immutable numeric GitHub account as `id:<number>`. A policy with
  zero patterns of a kind matches nothing -- fail-closed, no implicit wildcard;
  write `*` explicitly.
- For an exact repository/ref/SHA previously attested by Agent Host after a
  successful push, the resolved actor is the signed-in human. Otherwise it is
  the actor from GitHub's signed OIDC token. Both are retained in the audit log.
- A policy attached to a group grants every descendant leaf. Inheritance is
  additive: a leaf is vended if any matching policy sits on it or an ancestor.
- A machine token grants secrets by direct attachment to secret-tree nodes
  and/or via one optional bound policy (the union of both; the policy's
  repository/ref/actor patterns are never consulted for machine tokens). The
  token plaintext is shown once at creation and stored only as a SHA-256 hash.

## Using it from GitHub Actions

The composite action wraps the OIDC token request and the export:

    permissions:
      id-token: write

    jobs:
      deploy:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        steps:
          - uses: wow-look-at-my/actions@secret-server#latest
            id: secrets

          # Secrets are exported as masked environment variables
          - run: echo "Got $DB_URL"

## Admin surface (not for agents)

Everything under {{BASE_URL}}/admin/ (REST API + web UI) manages the secret
tree, policies, and machine tokens. It sits behind Cloudflare Access and is
meant for humans; agents should only ever call `/github/v1/secrets`. Every
secret access -- granted or denied -- is recorded in an audit log.

## More

- Full documentation (configuration, deployment, policy model):
  https://github.com/wow-look-at-my/secret-server
- Health check: GET {{BASE_URL}}/health (returns `ok`)
